title: Systems of Linear Equations
lead: A system is two or more equations that must be true at the same time. On the SAT you will see systems like 3x + 2y = 12 and y = 2x − 1, and be asked for a solution, one variable, or how many solutions exist. This is also the class where the Desmos intersection method becomes your biggest time-saver in Math.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
One linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions. For x + y = 7, the pairs (0, 7), (1, 6), (2, 5) and every other point on the line all work. A second equation narrows this down. Taken together, x + y = 7 and x − y = 3 are both true for only one pair: (5, 2).

So a system of two equations asks which point satisfies both at once. Geometrically: where do the two lines cross?

PictureWhat it meansSolutions
One intersectionThe lines cross onceOne (x, y) pair
Parallel linesSame slope, different interceptsNone
Same lineOne equation is a disguised copy of the otherInfinitely many

This mirrors Class 3. There, one equation simplified to a false statement (no solution) or a true one (infinitely many). With systems the same two special cases return as parallel and identical lines.

Every algebraic method has the same goal: turn two equations with two variables into one equation with one variable, which you already know how to solve from Class 3. There are two ways to do it, substitution and elimination.

parts.title: Part 2 · Substitution
parts.html:
Both equations are true at the same time, so if one equation tells you what a variable equals, you can replace that variable in the other equation with the same expression.

y=3x and x+y=8 The first equation says y is the same as 3x, so write 3x in place of y
x+3x=8 → 4x=8 → x=2
y=3(2)=6 → solution (2,6)

The steps:

  1. Isolate one variable in one of the equations, if it is not isolated already.
  2. Substitute that expression into the other equation. You now have one equation with one variable.
  3. Solve it.
  4. Go back to one of the original equations with that value to find the other variable.

When the substituted expression has two terms, keep it in parentheses so the multiplication reaches both.

y=2x−1 and 3x+2y=12 3x+2(2x−1)=12 → 3x+4x−2=12 → 7x=14 → x=2
y=2(2)−1=3 → solution (2,3)

If neither equation has a variable alone, isolate one yourself. Pick the variable with a coefficient of 1, because it will not create fractions.

x−3y=−5 and 4x−5y=1 Add 3y to both sides of the first → x=3y−5
Substitute into the second → 4(3y−5)−5y=1
12y−20−5y=1 → 7y=21 → y=3
x=3(3)−5=4 → solution (4,3)

parts.title: Part 3 · Elimination
parts.html:
You can add the same amount to both sides of an equation. The second equation says its left side and its right side are the same amount, so you can add its left side to the first equation’s left side and its right side to the first equation’s right side. If one variable has opposite coefficients in the two equations, it cancels.

3x+2y=12 and x−2y=−4 Add the equations: +2y and −2y cancel → 4x=8 → x=2
Substitute into the first → 3(2)+2y=12 → y=3 → solution (2,3)

Often nothing cancels as written. Then multiply one whole equation, both sides, by a number that makes a pair of coefficients match. There is usually more than one way to do it.

2x+y=9 and x+3y=12 Option 1, remove y: multiply the first by 3 → 6x+3y=27
Subtract the second → 5x=15 → x=3

Option 2, remove x: multiply the second by 2 → 2x+6y=24
Subtract the first → 5y=15 → y=3

Either way the solution is (3,3)

Matching coefficients with opposite signs cancel when you add. Matching coefficients with the same sign cancel when you subtract. When you subtract, change the sign of every term in the equation you are subtracting, including the constant.

The steps:

  1. Find a pair of terms with the same variable and coefficients of the same size, such as 2x and 2x, or 3y and −3y. If there is none, multiply one or both equations to create one.
  2. Add or subtract the equations so that pair cancels. You now have one equation with one variable.
  3. Solve it.
  4. Go back to either original equation with that value to find the other variable.

The answer does not have to be a whole number.

2x+3y=8 and 4x−3y=7 Add the equations: +3y and −3y cancel → 6x=15 → x=52
Substitute into the first → 2(52)+3y=8 → 5+3y=8 → y=1
Solution (52,1)

Verify. Plug the solution into both original equations. If it fails one, you made an arithmetic slip.

parts.title: Part 4 · Choosing a method
parts.html:
Every system of linear equations can be solved by substitution and by elimination, and both give the same answer. Use the one you are more comfortable with. These signs tell you which is likely to be quicker:

What you seeExampleQuicker method
A variable is already aloney = 5x − 2Substitution
A variable can be isolated in one step−2x + y = 9Substitution
Both equations contain the same term3x + 2y = 12 and 3x + 5y = 21Elimination, by subtracting
The equations contain opposite termsx + 4y = 9 and 6x − 4y = 5Elimination, by adding
One coefficient is a whole-number multiple of the other2x + 6y = 10 and 7x + 3y = 11Elimination, after multiplying the second equation by 2
The question asks for x + y or another combinationTry adding or subtracting the equations as they are
Awkward numbersDesmos (Part 6)

The same system can often be done both ways. For y = 2x and 5x + y = 14, you can substitute 2x for y to get 7x = 14. You can also rewrite the first equation as 2x − y = 0 and add it to the second, which again gives 7x = 14.

parts.title: Part 5 · How many solutions?
parts.html:
The solution of a system is the point where its two lines meet, and two lines can meet once, never, or everywhere. Which case you have depends only on the slopes and the y-intercepts:

Slopesy-interceptsThe linesSolutions
DifferentAnyCross onceOne
SameDifferentParallelNone
SameSameThe same lineInfinitely many

From a graph you can see this directly. Without a graph, do it with algebra:

  1. Rewrite both equations in slope-intercept form, y = mx + b.
  2. Compare the two m-values and the two b-values.
How many solutions does the system 2x+y=5 and 4x+2y=6 have? First equation → y=−2x+5
Second equation → 2y=−4x+6 → y=−2x+3
Same slope (−2), different intercepts (5 and 3) → parallel lines → no solution

The harder form of the question gives an unknown constant: “The system has no solution (or infinitely many solutions); what is the value of the constant?”

The rule: lines are parallel or identical when the x- and y-coefficients of one equation are the same multiple of the other's. Then the constants decide which case it is.

Example. 2x+3y=6 and 4x+6y=c Divide the second by 2 → 2x+3y=c2
c=12 → identical equations → infinitely many solutions
c≠12 → parallel lines → no solution

No value of c gives exactly one solution, because these lines can only be identical or parallel, never crossing. The SAT asks for this reasoning with uglier numbers.

Quick procedure. Divide the second equation by whatever makes its x-coefficient match the first's, then compare the remaining pieces.

parts.title: Part 6 · The Desmos method
parts.html:
This is the highest-value shortcut in the Math section. Type each equation on its own line in Desmos. Two lines appear; click the intersection point. The coordinates are the solution.

  • The question asks for x? Read the x-coordinate. For y, read the y-coordinate.
  • It asks for something built from the solution, like 2x + 3y? Compute it from the coordinates.
  • No solution shows as two parallel lines. Infinitely many shows as one visible line drawn twice.
  • For a system with an unknown constant, like ax + by = 12, graph what you know and use the given condition (a point the line passes through) to find the unknown.

When to still use algebra. When the question wants one variable and the setup is simple, elimination can be faster than typing two equations.

Tip. For “which ordered pair is the solution” questions with small numbers, plug in the choices. Test each pair in both equations; only one satisfies both. It is often 30 seconds in total and immune to sign errors.

parts.title: Part 7 · Systems in word problems
parts.html:
A word problem becomes a system when two quantities have two relationships.

A cinema sold 220 tickets. Adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $7, and total sales were $2100. Count: a+c=220
Money: 12a+7c=2100
Solution: a=112, c=108

The signal that you need a system: two unknowns and two independent facts about them. Count plus total cost is the classic pattern. It also appears as perimeter plus area, sum plus product, and speed-time-distance pairs.

Define the variables in words before writing equations. Write one equation per fact, in the order the facts appear. Then eliminate or use Desmos.

parts.title: Part 8 · Things to remember
parts.html:
• The goal is always one equation with one variable.
  • Substitution: isolate a variable, replace it in the other equation, solve, then go back for the second variable.
  • Elimination: make one pair of coefficients match, add or subtract the equations, solve, then go back for the second variable.
  • Number of solutions: put both equations in y = mx + b form and compare. Different slopes give one solution. The same slope with different y-intercepts gives none. The same slope and the same y-intercept give infinitely many.
  • Check the solution in both original equations.

parts.title: Part 9 · When the question asks for a combination
parts.html:
If a question asks for x + y, x − y or some other combination, try adding or subtracting the equations as they stand before solving for each variable.

3x + 2y = 17 and 2x + 3y = 13. What is the value of x + y? Add the equations → 5x+5y=30
Divide by 5 → x+y=6
Same system. What is the value of x − y? Subtract the second from the first → x−y=4

Check: the full solution is (5, 1), and 5 + 1 = 6, 5 − 1 = 4. The shortcut works whenever the coefficients in the sum or difference come out equal.
